summary: Mobility is stabilising at a near‑normal MF‑Index of 72, but public‑transport ridership remains below pre‑pandemic levels and real fuel‑saving outcomes are far short of theoretical potential. High‑risk sectors continue to drive travel, creating equity and economic exposure concerns that require targeted policy action.

signals.detail: Theoretical weekly savings of 35.7 M L contrast sharply with the measured 334 k L saved in the first week, representing less than 1% of the ceiling. This gap signals weak compliance and limited real‑world impact despite high fuel prices.

Daily PT trips total 1,235,713, projecting ~450 M trips annually—about 10% below the 2025 recovery level and 14% below 2019. While the ridership component scores 72.7, the downward trend threatens a shift back to private vehicles.

Retail & Services, Logistics and Construction sectors show low WFH (5‑15%) and high mobility scores (85‑95), sustaining fuel demand and congestion. Their exposure to volatile fuel prices amplifies macro‑economic risk.

Overall WFH adoption is 58.4%, yet it is uneven: public/GLC employees at 60% versus private professionals at 40% and high‑risk sectors under 15%. This disparity creates unequal burdens of travel costs and health exposure.

Fuel policy component is perfect (100) indicating strong price signals, but PT ridership remains depressed and fuel‑saving outcomes are minimal. Without complementary incentives, the anticipated modal shift to public transport is not materialising.

recommendation: Introduce a 10% fare subsidy and increase service frequency to lift daily PT ridership by Q4 2027, while mandating sector‑specific remote‑work targets of at least 30% for Retail, Logistics and Construction. Deploy a real‑time fuel‑savings monitoring platform to close the gap between theoretical and actual savings, enabling corrective policy adjustments.
